newsitem.title: UK: Iraq not telling full truth about weapons - U.N..
newsitem.headline: Iraq not telling full truth about weapons - U.N..

text.p: The head of the latest United Nations inspection team to visit Iraq said on Thursday his group had found clear evidence that Baghdad was still concealing the full extent of its secret weapons programme.
Colonel Terry Taylor said his 21-strong team uncovered an advanced biological weapons programme which the Iraqis had previously only hinted at.
"This hadn't been declared, so it's hard evidence that they're not telling us everything," he told reporters during a briefing held by the International Institute for Strategic Studies think-tank.

Taylor also expressed concern about signs the U.N. Security Council could relax sanctions imposed on Iraq after the 1990 invasion of Kuwait, saying he was convinced Baghdad would start up its weapons programme again as soon as measures were lifted.
"As long as you have the present regime in place, it's hard to imagine they wouldn't try again, given the extraordinary efforts they've made to hide evidence," he said.

Rolf Ekeus, head of the U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) in charge of Iraqi disarmament, accused Baghdad earlier this month of concealing small but significant quantities of banned weapons. Iraqi Prime Minister Tareq Aziz denied the charge on Wednesday.
Iraq is hardest hit by tight curbs on its oil exports which will not be fully lifted until UNSCOM confirms Baghdad has destroyed its weapons of mass destruction.
Since last December, Iraq has been allowed by the U.N. to export $2 billion worth of oil over six months, on a renewable basis, to pay for food, medicine and other humanitarian goods.
Taylor said his team had uncovered details of a weapons programme to produce a toxic agent during its April 5 to 20 assignment, but declined to give further details.
"What happens is that we find something out and they declare it. I am sure that after our mission they will declare they had a programme."
Taylor later made clear to Reuters that the Iraqis had briefly mentioned the programme to the U.N. team but had not revealed how advanced it was.

"Aziz is not telling the truth when he says the Iraqis have revealed everything," said Taylor, pouring scorn on the "draft full and final complete declarations" which Iraq is obliged to produce listing all its weapons of mass destruction.
"They've had four goes with the biological weapons programme and they've been plainly lacking in major elements. These are still lacking," he said.

Relaxing the sanctions would greatly benefit Russia, China and France, which have all recently signed oil exploration deals with Iraq that are on hold until the measures are lifted. Taylor said Turkey was also keen to resume trading with Baghdad.

"The resolve of the Security Council must be under question. I as an inspector have some concerns. (If we run into problems in Iraq) will I be supported 100 percent or will somebody let me down?" he said.
The difficult job of inspection teams would be made much harder if the punitive regime was lifted, he said.
"Even with the very intrusive inspections we do have, and they are very painful for those (Iraqis) concerned, it is difficult to be certain that major things are not being hidden."
Ekeus complained that the Iraqis had harrassed inspection teams, but Taylor said his escorts had given him no trouble.
